_comment: One free-response item per AP CSA lesson, exported from seed/csa-frq for
the printable teacher kit. Hidden test cases are deliberately excluded.

1.1.title: Introduction to Algorithms, Programming, and Compilers
1.1.name: Delivery Route
1.1.brief: An algorithm is an ordered sequence of steps, and on the exam the order is graded. This question hands you three leg distances and asks for four reported values, each of which depends on the ones before it. A student who computes the final answer in one expression gets that answer right and the intermediate rows wrong, which is exactly how partial credit is lost.
1.1.given: Three int variables legA, legB and legC are already declared and assigned for you. You do not declare them and you do not read any input.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the total distance of all three legs.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print the distance remaining after the first leg is driven.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the average leg distance as an int, using integer division.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the length of the longest single leg, using Math.max.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines, one per rubric part, in order (a) through (d).
Part (c) is integer division on purpose. 100 / 3 is 33, not 33.333, and the exam expects 33.
Part (d) has no if statement available to you. Math.max takes two arguments, so use it twice.
1.1.starter:
// legA, legB and legC are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: total, remaining after leg A, average (integer), longest leg.
hints: Compute the total once into a variable and reuse it. Part (b) is the total minus legA, and writing legB + legC instead is correct here but stops being correct the moment the question changes.
Integer division truncates toward zero. There is no rounding in part (c) and no cast to double: 25 / 2 is 12.
Math.max only compares two values. Math.max(a, Math.max(b, c)) compares all three without a single if.

1.2.title: Variables and Data Types
1.2.name: Concert Inventory
1.2.brief: The exam does not ask you to name a data type. It asks you to compute something, and then scores whether the type you chose held the answer. An int that should have been a double loses the fraction silently, and a boolean printed as text is the only way to show a yes or no answer before selection is taught.
1.2.given: Three variables are declared and assigned for you: int seats, int sold and double price.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the number of seats still unsold, as an int.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print the total revenue from the seats sold, as a double.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the revenue that the remaining seats would add if they all sold.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print a boolean: true when the show is completely sold out.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Part (b) and part (c) are money. They must print with a decimal point, which means the expression has to be a double and not an int.
Part (d) has no if statement. A comparison IS a boolean value, so you can print the comparison itself.
1.2.starter:
// seats, sold and price are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: unsold seats, revenue so far, revenue remaining, sold out or not.
hints: An int times a double is a double, so sold * price already prints with a decimal point. You do not need a cast and you should not store it in an int.
Part (d) does not need an if. System.out.println(unsold == 0) prints the words true or false, which is what the question asks for.
Compute unsold once. Parts (a), (c) and (d) all depend on it, and three separate subtractions is three chances to write one of them backwards.

1.3.title: Expressions and Output
1.3.name: Scoreboard Line
1.3.brief: Half the free response points lost on output questions are lost to the difference between print and println, and to concatenation that silently turns arithmetic into text. "Score: " + 2 + 3 is "Score: 23". This question is built around that.
1.3.given: Four variables are declared for you: String team, int made, int missed and int bonus.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the team name followed by a colon, a space, and the number of shots made, on one line.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print the total number of shots attempted.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the score, counting two points per shot made plus the bonus.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the team name and the score joined by a space, on one line.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
In part (a) and part (d) the number must be the computed value, not the digits stuck together. Parentheses decide that.
Nothing here needs an if or a loop.
1.3.starter:
// team, made, missed and bonus are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines. Watch what + does when a String is on the left.
hints: Once a String appears on the left of a +, every + after it concatenates. "x" + 2 + 3 is "x23". Wrap the arithmetic in parentheses, or compute it into a variable first, which is what the reference does.
Part (b) has no String in it at all, so made + missed is ordinary addition and prints as one number.
println moves to a new line and print does not. Four printed lines means four println calls, not four print calls.

1.4.title: Assignment Statements and Input
1.4.name: Locker Assignment
1.4.brief: Assignment is not equality, and the order of assignments is the algorithm. This question walks a value through four reassignments and asks you to report it at each stage, which is the shape of every FRQ part that says "after the code segment executes".
1.4.given: Two variables are declared and assigned for you: int locker and int shift.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the starting locker number.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Move the locker forward by shift, then print it.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Double the locker number, then print it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Move it back by shift, then print it.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Each part changes the SAME variable and then prints it. Do not print a fresh expression each time: the point of the question is that the value carries forward.
Part (d) is the value after parts (b) and (c) have already happened, not the starting value minus shift.
1.4.starter:
// locker and shift are already declared and assigned.
// Report the locker number after each change, four lines in all.
hints: locker = locker + shift reads right to left: work out the right side with the current value, then store the result back. It is not an equation and it is not a claim that the two sides are equal.
If your four printed lines can be worked out without knowing the previous one, you have written four independent expressions and the third and fourth will be wrong.
Part (d) subtracts from the DOUBLED value. (start + shift) * 2 - shift is not the same as start + shift * 2 - shift.

1.5.title: Casting and Range of Variables
1.5.name: Fuel Economy Report
1.5.brief: Casting is the single most reliable place to lose an FRQ point, because the wrong answer looks right. (double) (a / b) casts AFTER the integer division has already thrown the fraction away. This question asks for the same quotient three different ways so the difference is on the page.
1.5.given: Two variables are declared and assigned for you: int miles and int gallons.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print miles per gallon using integer division, so the fraction is discarded.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print miles per gallon as an exact double.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the miles left over that the whole number in part (a) does not account for.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the exact result from part (b) rounded down to an int by casting.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Part (b) must cast BEFORE the division, not after. Casting the result of int division is too late.
Part (c) is the remainder operator. Part (d) is a cast applied to the double from part (b).
1.5.starter:
// miles and gallons are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: integer mpg, exact mpg, leftover miles, exact mpg cast back to int.
hints: (double) miles / gallons casts miles first, so the division is double division. (double) (miles / gallons) divides as ints first and then converts the already truncated answer, which is the classic lost point.
The remainder operator % gives what is left after integer division. miles / gallons and miles % gallons together account for every mile.
Casting a double to an int truncates toward zero. It does not round: (int) 9.98 is 9.

1.6.title: Compound Assignment Operators
1.6.name: Register Receipt
1.6.brief: Compound assignment is not shorthand for the exam; it is where the exam plants truncation. total *= 108 / 100 is not an 8 percent increase, because 108 / 100 is 1. This question is a receipt computed entirely in cents so that every rounding decision is one you make on purpose.
1.6.given: Five variables are declared and assigned for you: int a, b, c and d are item prices in cents, and int paidCents is what the customer handed over.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the subtotal in cents.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print the average item price in cents as a double.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print 8 percent tax on the subtotal, in cents, truncated.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the whole dollars of change, then on the next line the leftover cents. Change is what is left after BOTH the subtotal and the tax.

task: Write a code segment that prints five lines: subtotal, average, tax, dollars of change, leftover cents.
Part (c) is 8 percent truncated, so multiply before you divide. subtotal * 8 / 100 truncates once at the end; subtotal * (8 / 100) is always zero.
Change is paidCents minus the subtotal minus the tax. Forgetting the tax is the mistake this part is looking for. Dollars is integer division by 100 and leftover cents is the remainder.
1.6.starter:
// a, b, c, d and paidCents are already declared and assigned.
// Print five lines: subtotal, average, tax, dollars of change, leftover cents.
hints: Multiply before dividing whenever the divisor is bigger than the numerator. subtotal * 8 / 100 keeps the precision until the last step; anything that computes 8 / 100 first gets 0.
Part (b) needs a cast before the division or the average of 99, 100, 101 and 102 prints as 100 instead of 100.5.
Dollars and cents come from the same value: change / 100 and change % 100. Computing them from two different expressions is how they stop agreeing.
The customer pays the tax too. Change is paidCents - subtotal - tax, and a receipt that hands back the tax as change is the bug this part exists to catch.

1.7.title: Application Program Interface (API) and Libraries
1.7.name: Sensor Calibration
1.7.brief: An API is a promise about what a method returns, and the exam grades whether you read the promise or guessed at it. Math.abs returns the magnitude, Math.pow returns a double even when both arguments look like ints, and Integer.parseInt throws rather than returning zero. Each part here is one library call whose documented return type decides the answer.
1.7.given: Three variables are declared and assigned for you: int reading, int target and String rawCount.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print how far the reading is from the target, as a distance that is never negative.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print the reading squared, using Math.pow.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the raw count converted from text to a number, then multiplied by two.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the smaller of the reading and the target.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Part (b) uses Math.pow, which is documented to return a double. Print what it actually returns; do not cast it to an int.
Part (c) needs Integer.parseInt. A String of digits is not a number until something converts it.
1.7.starter:
// reading, target and rawCount are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: distance from target, reading squared, parsed count doubled, smaller value.
hints: Math.abs(reading - target) works whichever value is larger, which is why the question asks for a distance rather than a difference. Subtracting in one fixed order is right half the time.
Math.pow returns a double. 5 squared prints as 25.0 and not 25, and that is the documented behaviour rather than a bug to correct.
Integer.parseInt turns a String of digits into an int. Multiplying the String by 2 does not compile, and concatenating it with itself is not doubling it.

1.8.title: Documentation with Comments
1.8.name: Precondition Contract
1.8.brief: Documentation on the exam is not a comment you write, it is a contract you are held to. A precondition tells you what you may ASSUME, and every point lost to "but what if the input is negative" is a point lost to code defending against a case the documentation already ruled out. This question states its preconditions and then scores whether you trusted them.
1.8.given: Three variables are declared and assigned for you: int boxes, int perBox and int shipped. Preconditions: boxes is at least 1, perBox is at least 1, and shipped is between 0 and boxes * perBox inclusive.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the total number of items across all boxes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print how many items are still unshipped.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the number of FULL boxes the unshipped items would fill.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the percentage shipped, truncated to a whole number.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
The preconditions guarantee perBox is at least 1, so part (c) and part (d) never divide by zero. You do not need to check for it, and the exam does not award a point for checking.
Part (d) is shipped * 100 / total, which truncates once at the end. Dividing first gives 0 every time.
hints: A precondition is a promise made TO you. You may assume perBox is at least 1 and write the division directly.
Part (c) asks for FULL boxes, which is what integer division already gives you. 7 items at 3 per box is 2 full boxes, not 2.33 and not 3.
Part (d) must multiply before it divides. shipped / total is 0 for every input where shipped is smaller than total, so multiplying that by 100 is still 0.

1.9.title: Method Signatures
1.9.name: Match the Signature
1.9.brief: This is the first question on the course that scores you on the signature rather than the body. The methods below are called by code you cannot see and cannot edit, so a method that prints instead of returning, or takes its parameters in the other order, fails every case no matter how correct the arithmetic inside it is. That is precisely how the exam works.
1.9.given: Nothing is given. You write a class named Ticket containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method: a hidden driver calls your methods and prints what they return.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int total(int adults, int children) returns the number of people.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int cost(int people, int pricePer) returns people times pricePer.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static double average(int collected, int people) returns collected divided by people as an exact double.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static String label(String event, int people) returns the event, a space, then the number of people.

task: Write class Ticket with the four static methods exactly as their signatures describe. No main method.
Every method RETURNS its answer. A method that prints the answer and returns nothing does not compile against the driver, because the driver uses the returned value.
Part (c) divides two ints and must not truncate, so cast before dividing. The parameter order is collected then people, not people then collected.
hints: A signature is the name, the parameter types and their ORDER. average(int collected, int people) called with the people first still compiles and still returns the wrong number, which is why the exam writes the order down.
return hands a value back to whoever called. System.out.println shows it to a human. The driver needs the first one; printing inside your method adds a stray line to the output and returns nothing.
Part (c) is (double) collected / people. Casting the whole quotient instead, as (double) (collected / people), truncates first and then converts the already ruined answer.

1.10.title: Calling Class Methods
1.10.name: Static Call Chain
1.10.brief: A class method is called on the CLASS, not on an object, and the return value is the only thing that comes back. The most common lost point in this topic is a call whose result is thrown away: Math.max(a, b); on its own line computes the maximum and discards it.
1.10.given: Three variables are declared and assigned for you: int first, int second and String code.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the larger of first and second.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print the square root of the larger value.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the length of code.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print code with every letter in upper case.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Math and Integer methods are called on the class. String methods like length and toUpperCase are called on the object.
Every one of these RETURNS a value. A call on a line by itself computes an answer and throws it away.
1.10.starter:
// first, second and code are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: larger value, its square root, length of code, code upper cased.
hints: Store the larger value once and reuse it. Part (a) and part (b) both need it, and calling Math.max twice is two chances to swap the arguments.
Math.sqrt returns a double, so the answer prints with a decimal point even when the root is a whole number. 16 gives 4.0.
toUpperCase does not change the String it is called on, because a String cannot be changed. It RETURNS a new one, so code.toUpperCase(); on its own line does nothing at all.

1.11.title: Math Class
1.11.name: Random Range and Rounding
1.11.brief: Math is the one library the exam expects from memory, and it has three traps in it: pow returns a double, integer division inside a Math call happens before Math ever sees it, and casting a double to an int truncates rather than rounding. This question walks through all three with no randomness, so every answer is checkable.
1.11.given: Three variables are declared and assigned for you: int base, int exponent and double measurement.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print base raised to the exponent.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print that same power converted to an int by casting.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print measurement rounded to the nearest whole number using Math.round.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print measurement truncated toward zero by casting.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Parts (c) and (d) are the same number treated two different ways, and they disagree whenever the fraction is one half or more. That disagreement is the point of the question.
Math.round on a double returns a long. Printing it directly is correct.
1.11.starter:
// base, exponent and measurement are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: the power, the power as an int, the rounded measurement, the truncated measurement.
hints: Math.pow always returns a double, so part (a) prints with a decimal point even for 2 to the 3rd. Part (b) is where it becomes an int.
Casting truncates toward zero and never rounds. (int) 7.99 is 7. Math.round(7.99) is 8. A question that asks for both is asking you to show you know the difference.
Compute the power once into a variable. Parts (a) and (b) are the same value shown two ways, and calling Math.pow twice invites a typo in one of them.

1.12.title: Objects: Instances of Classes
1.12.name: Two References, One Object
1.12.brief: An object is not its variable. Two names can point at the same object, and two separate objects can hold equal contents while == says they are different things. This is the single most tested idea in the whole unit and it is where == on Strings comes from.
1.12.given: Three String variables are declared and assigned for you: a, b and c. a and b are built from the same literal; c is built with new.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print whether a and b are the same object, using ==.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print whether a and c are the same object, using ==.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print whether a and c hold the same characters, using equals.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the length of c.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Parts (a) and (b) ask about identity, which is what == compares for objects. Part (c) asks about contents, which is what equals compares.
Do not use an if. A comparison is already a boolean and can be printed directly.
1.12.starter:
// a, b and c are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: a == b, a == c, a.equals(c), and the length of c.
hints: For objects, == asks "is this the very same object in memory", not "do these look alike". Two Strings with identical characters can be two different objects.
new ALWAYS makes a new object. That is why a == c is false even though the characters match, and it is the whole reason equals exists.
You do not need an if for any part. System.out.println(a == b) prints true or false by itself.

1.13.title: Object Creation and Storage (Instantiation)
1.13.name: Immutable Strings
1.13.brief: Creating an object and changing a variable are different acts. A String can never be changed, so every method that looks like it edits one is really building a new one and handing it back. A student who calls the method and does not store the result has created an object and thrown it away, and the exam scores exactly that.
1.13.given: Two variables are declared and assigned for you: String word and String suffix.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print word unchanged.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Build a new String from word and suffix joined together, and print it.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print word again, to show it did not change.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the length of the joined String.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Part (c) must print the ORIGINAL word. If your part (b) changed word itself, part (c) will disagree with part (a) and both cannot be right.
Store the joined String in its own variable. Parts (b) and (d) both need it.
1.13.starter:
// word and suffix are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: word, the joined String, word again, and the joined length.
hints: Parts (a) and (c) print the same thing, on purpose. That is the evidence that building a new String left the original alone.
word = word + suffix would make part (c) print the joined value and lose the point. Assign to a NEW variable instead.
Part (d) is the length of the joined String, not of word. Store the join once and ask that variable for its length.

1.14.title: Calling Instance Methods
1.14.name: Reading a Record
1.14.brief: An instance method is called ON an object and usually answers a question about that particular object. The exam grades whether you called it on the right one: two objects of the same type accept the same calls, and asking the wrong object is a mistake that compiles cleanly and gives a plausible wrong answer.
1.14.given: Two String variables are declared and assigned for you: title and author.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the first character of title.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print the number of characters in author.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print the last character of author.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print title in lower case.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Watch which object each part asks. Parts (a) and (d) are about title; parts (b) and (c) are about author.
The last character sits at index length() - 1, because indexes start at 0.
1.14.starter:
// title and author are already declared and assigned.
// Print four lines: first char of title, length of author, last char of author, title lower cased.
hints: charAt(0) is the first character, not charAt(1). Indexes start at zero, so the last one is length() - 1.
Read each part again and check which variable it names. title.length() compiles perfectly and answers a question nobody asked.
toLowerCase returns a new String rather than changing title. Print what it returns.

1.15.title: String Manipulation
1.15.name: Split a Record Line
1.15.brief: substring and indexOf together are the most heavily tested pair in Unit 1, and the exam always tests the same boundary: substring(a, b) includes a and EXCLUDES b. Off by one here is not a typo, it is the whole question.
1.15.given: One variable is declared and assigned for you: String record, which always contains exactly one comma, with at least one character on each side of it.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Print the position of the comma.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Print everything before the comma.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Print everything after the comma.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Print the total number of characters that are not the comma.

task: Write a code segment that prints four lines in rubric order.
Neither part (b) nor part (c) may include the comma itself. substring(0, i) stops just before index i, and substring(i + 1) starts just after it.
The precondition guarantees there is exactly one comma, so part (d) is the length minus one.
1.15.starter:
// record is already declared and assigned, and contains exactly one comma.
// Print four lines: comma position, text before it, text after it, characters that are not the comma.
hints: substring(0, at) gives characters 0 through at - 1, which is everything before the comma and not the comma. Using at + 1 as the end includes it.
The one argument form, substring(at + 1), runs to the end of the String. There is no need to pass length() as a second argument, though it is not wrong to.
Store indexOf once. Parts (a), (b) and (c) all need the same position, and calling indexOf three times is three chances to write one of them differently.

2.1.title: Algorithms with Selection and Repetition
2.1.name: Step Counter
2.1.brief: An algorithm that repeats and an algorithm that chooses are the two halves of this unit, and the exam almost always asks for them together: loop over a range, decide something about each value, and report a total. Getting the loop right and the condition backwards still scores zero, which is why each part here isolates one of them.
2.1.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Steps containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method: a hidden driver calls your methods.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int sumTo(int n) returns 1 + 2 + ... + n, and 0 when n is less than 1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int countEvens(int n) returns how many of 1 through n are even.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static String verdict(int score) returns "PASS" when score is 60 or more, otherwise "FAIL".

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int firstMultiple(int start, int step) returns the smallest multiple of step that is at least start. Assume step is at least 1 and start is at least 0.

task: Write class Steps with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Part (a) must return 0 rather than crash when n is 0 or negative. A loop that never runs already does this, so you may not need a special case at all.
Every method RETURNS its answer. A method that prints it and returns nothing does not compile against the driver.
hints: A for loop that starts at 1 and runs while i <= n never executes when n is 0 or negative, so part (a) returns its starting total of 0 with no extra check.
Part (c) is a boundary question. 60 itself must be a PASS, so the test is >= and not >.
Part (d) already answers correctly when start is 0, because 0 is a multiple of every step. Starting the search at step instead of 0 gets that one case wrong.

2.2.title: Boolean Expressions
2.2.name: Range Checks
2.2.brief: A boolean method has only two possible answers, which makes it the easiest kind of method to get accidentally right. Every part here is checked from both sides, because a method that always returns true is correct on half the inputs and worth no points.
2.2.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Checks containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static boolean isPositive(int n) returns whether n is greater than zero.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static boolean inRange(int n, int low, int high) returns whether n is between low and high, inclusive of both.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static boolean isMultiple(int n, int factor) returns whether n divides evenly by factor. Assume factor is not zero.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static boolean sameParity(int a, int b) returns whether a and b are both even or both odd.

task: Write class Checks with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
None of these needs an if statement. A comparison already IS a boolean, so return the comparison itself.
Part (b) is inclusive at both ends. low and high are each inside the range.
hints: if (x > 0) { return true; } else { return false; } is the long way of writing return x > 0. Both are correct; only one of them is the point of this lesson.
Inclusive means the endpoints count. Using > and < instead of >= and <= excludes exactly the two values most likely to be tested.
Two numbers have the same parity when both remainders match. Comparing a % 2 to b % 2 handles that in one expression without four separate cases.

2.3.title: if Statements
2.3.name: Shipping Tiers
2.3.brief: A tiered rule is the most common if question on the exam, and it has one trap: the order of the branches. Written from the loosest condition down, every input falls into the first branch and the rest are unreachable. The tiers here are arranged so that mistake changes the answer.
2.3.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Shipping containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int fee(int weight) returns 5 when weight is under 10, 10 when weight is under 50, and 20 otherwise.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static String size(int weight) returns "SMALL" under 10, "MEDIUM" under 50, and "LARGE" otherwise.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int discounted(int fee, boolean member) returns half the fee (integer division) for a member, and the full fee otherwise.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int total(int weight, boolean member) returns the discounted fee for that weight.

task: Write class Shipping with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Part (d) must call your own part (a) and part (c) rather than repeating their rules. A tier rule written twice is a tier rule that will disagree with itself later.
"Under 10" means strictly less than 10. A weight of exactly 10 is in the middle tier.
hints: Check the tightest condition first. If you test weight < 50 before weight < 10, then a weight of 3 is under 50 and takes the middle tier, and the small tier can never be reached.
A boolean parameter does not need == true. if (member) is the whole condition.
Part (d) is one line if you reuse the methods you already wrote. Copying the tier rules into it is how the two versions drift apart when a price changes.

2.4.title: Nested if Statements
2.4.name: Admission Rules
2.4.brief: Nesting is where the dangling else lives. An else belongs to the NEAREST unmatched if, not to the one it lines up with on the page, and indentation has no effect on which. This question has a case for every leaf of the decision tree so a misattached else cannot hide.
2.4.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Admission containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static String tier(int age) returns "CHILD" under 13, "TEEN" under 20, "ADULT" under 65, and "SENIOR" otherwise.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int price(int age) returns 0 for CHILD, 8 for TEEN, 15 for ADULT and 10 for SENIOR.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static boolean needsGuardian(int age, boolean afterSix) returns true only when the visitor is a CHILD, or is a TEEN and it is after six.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int charge(int age, boolean afterSix) returns the price, plus 5 when a guardian is needed.

task: Write class Admission with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Part (b) and part (c) should decide the tier by calling your part (a) rather than repeating the age boundaries. Four boundaries written three times is twelve chances to mistype one.
Every boundary is exclusive at the top: 13 is a TEEN, 20 is an ADULT, 65 is a SENIOR.
hints: Compare Strings with equals, never with ==. Two Strings holding the same characters can be different objects, and == asks whether they are the same object.
Part (c) is true for every CHILD regardless of the hour, and for a TEEN only after six. An ADULT is never true, whatever the hour.
Build each method on the one before it. If part (a) is right, parts (b), (c) and (d) never need to mention 13, 20 or 65 at all.

2.5.title: Compound Boolean Expressions
2.5.name: Eligibility
2.5.brief: The exam tests && and || by making one of them wrong in a way that is right most of the time. Swapping && for || in a two condition rule gives the same answer on three of the four combinations. Every part here has a case for the combination that separates them.
2.5.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Eligible containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static boolean canDrive(int age, boolean hasLicense) returns whether the person is at least 16 AND has a license.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static boolean freeEntry(int age, boolean member) returns whether the person is under 6 OR is a member.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static boolean needsReview(int score, int absences) returns whether the score is under 70 OR absences are over 10.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static boolean honorRoll(int score, int absences) returns whether the score is at least 90 AND absences are at most 3.

task: Write class Eligible with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
None of these needs an if. Return the compound expression itself.
Read each boundary carefully: "at least 16" is >= 16, "under 6" is < 6, "over 10" is > 10, "at most 3" is <= 3.
hints: && needs both sides true. || needs only one. Read the sentence again: "and" versus "or" is the whole question.
A rule with two conditions has four combinations. Test all four in your head before you submit: true/true, true/false, false/true, false/false.
"At most 3" includes 3 itself, so it is <= 3. Writing < 3 silently excludes the student with exactly three absences.

2.6.title: Comparing Boolean Expressions
2.6.name: De Morgan in Practice
2.6.brief: Two boolean expressions are equivalent when they agree on EVERY input, and the exam tests that with the one rule students reliably get backwards: not (A and B) is (not A) OR (not B), never (not A) and (not B). This question asks for the same rule written both ways so they can be compared directly.
2.6.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Logic containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static boolean bothOpen(boolean a, boolean b) returns whether both are true.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static boolean notBothOpen(boolean a, boolean b) returns the opposite of part (a), written WITHOUT calling part (a).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static boolean neitherOpen(boolean a, boolean b) returns whether both are false.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static boolean onlyFirstOpen(boolean a, boolean b) returns whether a is true and b is false.

task: Write class Logic with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Parts (b) and (c) are DIFFERENT rules and the driver will show you where they differ. "Not both" is true when one is open; "neither" is not.
Part (d) is true only for the first door. It is deliberately not symmetric: onlyFirstOpen(true, false) and onlyFirstOpen(false, true) must give different answers.
hints: Distributing a not across an and flips the connector too. !(a && b) is !a || !b. Writing !a && !b gives you "neither", which is a different rule that happens to agree when both are false.
Part (d) needs both halves: a must be true AND b must be false. Returning a alone is right on three of the four rows, which is exactly the kind of nearly correct that a full truth table catches.
Fill in the four row truth table for your parts (b) and (c) before submitting. They must disagree on two of the four rows.

2.7.title: while Loops
2.7.name: Digit Machine
2.7.brief: A while loop is the right tool when you do not know the count in advance, which is exactly the case for taking a number apart digit by digit. The trap is the zero case: a loop written as "while there are digits left" runs zero times for the number 0 and reports that 0 has no digits.
2.7.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Digits containing exactly the four static methods described below. Assume every argument is zero or positive. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int count(int n) returns how many digits n has. The number 0 has one digit.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int sum(int n) returns the sum of the digits of n.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int lastDigit(int n) returns the final digit of n.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int reverse(int n) returns n with its digits reversed. Leading zeros simply disappear, so 100 reverses to 1.

task: Write class Digits with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Part (a) must return 1 for the number 0. A plain while (n > 0) loop returns 0, which is the bug this part is about.
Every loop here must change n, or it will never end. The verifier gives up after fifteen seconds and reports a timeout, not a wrong answer.
hints: n % 10 gives the last digit and n / 10 removes it. Those two together are the whole technique for every part here.
Part (a) is the only one that needs a special case, because 0 has a digit but no digits greater than zero to loop over.
Part (d) builds its answer by multiplying by 10 and adding the next digit. Adding first and multiplying after gives a different, wrong number.

2.8.title: for Loops
2.8.name: Accumulator Identities
2.8.brief: Every accumulator starts at its identity: 0 for a sum, 1 for a product, and the FIRST value for a maximum. Starting a maximum at 0 is the most common accumulator bug on the exam, and it is invisible until every value happens to be negative.
2.8.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Totals containing exactly the four static methods described below. Assume count is at least 1. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int sumRange(int low, int high) returns the sum of every integer from low to high inclusive, and 0 when low is greater than high.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int product(int n) returns 1 times 2 times ... times n, and 1 when n is less than 1.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int largestMultiple(int limit, int step) returns the largest multiple of step that is at most limit. Assume step is at least 1 and limit is at least 0.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int countDivisors(int n) returns how many integers from 1 to n divide n evenly. Assume n is at least 1.

task: Write class Totals with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Part (b) starts its accumulator at 1, not 0. A product that starts at 0 stays 0 forever.
Every loop here counts up to a known bound, which is what a for loop is for.
hints: A sum starts at 0 and a product starts at 1. Those are the values that leave the answer unchanged when nothing is combined into them, which is why they are called identities.
Part (a) returns 0 for an empty range without a special case, because a for loop whose condition is false at the start never runs.
Part (c) needs no loop at all. Integer division already truncates to a whole number of steps, so limit / step * step is the answer.

2.9.title: Implementing Selection and Iteration Algorithms
2.9.name: Running Statistics
2.9.brief: This is the shape of a real free response question: loop over values, keep several running answers at once, and report them. The maximum here is seeded with the first value rather than with zero, because the data can be entirely negative and a zero seed would report a maximum that never appeared in the input.
2.9.given: The driver reads a count and then that many integers, and passes them to your methods one call at a time is NOT how this works: each method receives the count and reads nothing. Instead each method is given the values it needs as parameters. Write a class named Stats containing exactly the four static methods described below. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int betterMax(int running, int next) returns whichever of the two is larger.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int rangeSum(int low, int high, int skip) returns the sum of low through high inclusive, leaving out any value that divides evenly by skip. Assume skip is at least 2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int countAbove(int low, int high, int threshold) returns how many integers from low to high inclusive are strictly greater than threshold.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int firstAbove(int low, int high, int threshold) returns the first integer from low upward that is strictly greater than threshold, or high + 1 if there is none.

task: Write class Stats with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Part (d) must stop at the FIRST match. A loop that keeps going and overwrites its answer returns the last match instead.
"Strictly greater" excludes the threshold itself in both part (c) and part (d).
hints: Part (a) is where a running maximum comes from. Returning next when it is strictly greater keeps the EARLIER value on a tie, which is usually what a question means by "the first largest".
Part (d) returns from inside the loop. That is what makes it stop at the first match rather than the last.
Part (b) skips a value when it divides evenly, so the condition to KEEP a value is i % skip != 0.

2.10.title: Implementing String Algorithms
2.10.name: Scanning a String
2.10.brief: Every String algorithm on the exam is a loop from 0 to length() - 1 with charAt inside it. The two ways to lose the point are looping to length() (which throws) and comparing characters with equals (which does not compile for a char).
2.10.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Scan containing exactly the four static methods described below. Assume every String argument is not null. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int countChar(String s, String target) returns how many times the first character of target appears in s. Assume target has at least one character.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static String reverse(String s) returns s with its characters in the opposite order.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static boolean isPalindrome(String s) returns whether s reads the same forwards and backwards. The empty String is a palindrome.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int countVowels(String s) returns how many of the characters a, e, i, o and u appear in s, lower case only.

task: Write class Scan with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
A loop over a String runs from 0 while i < s.length(). Using <= reads one character past the end and throws.
Characters compare with ==, not equals. s.charAt(i) == 'a' is the comparison; s.charAt(i).equals("a") does not compile.
hints: The last valid index is length() - 1. A loop that runs while i <= s.length() throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on the very last pass.
Building a String by adding characters one at a time is fine here. Start with the empty String, which is the identity for concatenation exactly as 0 is for a sum.
Part (c) is one line once part (b) works. A palindrome is a String equal to its own reversal, and reusing your own method is both shorter and harder to get wrong.

2.11.title: Nested Iteration
2.11.name: Rows and Columns
2.11.brief: A nested loop multiplies. The outer loop body runs once per row, the inner one runs fully inside each of those, and the counter that belongs to the outer loop must not be reset by the inner one. Every rectangle here is deliberately NOT square, because a square hides a swapped pair of bounds completely.
2.11.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Grid containing exactly the four static methods described below. Assume rows and cols are each at least 1. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int cells(int rows, int cols) returns how many cells a rows by cols rectangle has.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int sumProducts(int rows, int cols) returns the sum of r times c over every r from 1 to rows and every c from 1 to cols.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int countPairs(int n) returns how many ordered pairs (i, j) with 1 <= i < j <= n exist.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static String rowLabel(int row, int cols) returns the numbers 1 through cols each multiplied by row, separated by single spaces, with no space at the start.

task: Write class Grid with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Part (a) and part (b) both use a nested loop. Count the cells rather than assuming the shape is square.
Part (d) separates the numbers with single spaces and must not begin with one. Adding the separator BEFORE each item except the first is the usual way.
hints: The accumulator belongs OUTSIDE both loops. Declaring it inside the outer loop resets it on every row and reports only the last row.
Part (c) starts its inner loop at i + 1, which is what makes each pair count once rather than twice.
Part (d) adds the space before each item after the first. Dropping the c > 1 guard puts a space at the very start of the line, which the driver does compare.

2.12.title: Informal Run-Time Analysis
2.12.name: Counting the Work
2.12.brief: Run-time analysis on this exam is literal: how many times does the statement inside the loop actually execute? Rather than asking for a name like "quadratic", this question asks you to COUNT, which is the same skill without the vocabulary in the way, and it is checkable.
2.12.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Work containing exactly the four static methods described below. Assume n is at least 0. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int singleLoop(int n) returns how many times the body of a loop running i from 0 while i < n executes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int nestedLoop(int n) returns how many times the inner body executes when both loops run from 0 while less than n.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int triangleLoop(int n) returns how many times the inner body executes when the inner loop starts at i + 1 and runs while less than n.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int halvingLoop(int n) returns how many times the body executes when the counter starts at n and is halved by integer division until it reaches 0.

task: Write class Work with the four static methods exactly as described. No main method.
Write the loops and count, rather than reasoning out a formula. The point of this lesson is that the count is something you can determine exactly.
Part (d) must terminate. Halving by integer division reaches 0 from any starting value, but only if the counter actually changes on every pass.
hints: Part (b) is n times n and part (c) is about half of that. Comparing the two numbers the driver prints is the whole insight of this lesson: the same nesting can do very different amounts of work.
Every part returns 0 for n of 0, because none of the loops run. That is worth checking, because a formula written from memory often does not.
Part (d) grows very slowly. Doubling n adds ONE step, which is what makes halving so much better than counting down by one.

3.1.title: Abstraction and Program Design
3.1.name: One Place for Each Fact
3.1.brief: Abstraction on the exam means the caller does not get to know how you stored anything. This class is asked for two facts that are really one: a total and a count. Store both and they will disagree the first time something changes; store the ingredients and compute the rest, and they cannot.
3.1.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Tally. Do not write a main method: a hidden driver constructs your object, calls its methods, and prints what it observes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Tally() that starts with nothing recorded.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public void add(int value) records one more value.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public int getCount() returns how many values have been recorded, and public int getTotal() returns their sum.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public int getAverage() returns the total divided by the count using integer division, and 0 when nothing has been recorded.

task: Write class Tally with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
Part (d) must not divide by zero. A Tally with nothing in it returns 0 rather than crashing.
Do not store the average. It is computed from the total and the count, and a stored copy is a third fact that can disagree with the other two.
hints: The driver builds an EMPTY Tally first and asks it for an average. If your getAverage divides without checking, that call throws ArithmeticException before anything else is printed.
add changes two fields at once. Forgetting to increment the count gives a total that looks right and an average that is wildly wrong, with no error message.
Integer division is what the question asks for. 7 / 2 is 3, and no rounding is wanted.

3.2.title: Impact of Program Design
3.2.name: Changing the Rule in One Place
3.2.brief: A design is good when a rule change touches one method. This class applies the same threshold in three places, and the question is written so that a student who copies the comparison three times still passes the visible cases and fails the hidden one where the threshold is different.
3.2.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Grader. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Grader(int threshold) that remembers the passing threshold.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public boolean passes(int score) returns whether score is at least the threshold.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public String label(int score) returns "PASS" or "FAIL", decided by part (b).

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public int countPassing(int a, int b, int c) returns how many of the three scores pass, decided by part (b).

task: Write class Grader with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
Parts (c) and (d) must call part (b). The threshold comparison is written ONCE, in passes.
"At least" includes the threshold itself.
hints: The driver builds a SECOND Grader with a different threshold and asks it the same question. A comparison hardcoded to 60 passes the first object and fails the second.
this.threshold = threshold; is how a constructor parameter and a field with the same name are told apart. Writing threshold = threshold; assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field at 0.
countPassing is three calls to passes. Repeating the comparison inside it is the design mistake the second Grader is there to catch.

3.3.title: Anatomy of a Class
3.3.name: Fields, Not Locals
3.3.brief: The difference between a field and a local variable is the difference between a class that remembers and one that does not, and Java will not warn you which you wrote. A local declared inside a method shadows the field of the same name, the method compiles, and every getter afterwards returns the field it never touched.
3.3.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Locker. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Locker(String owner, int capacity) that stores both.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public String getOwner() and public int getCapacity() return what was stored.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public void store(int items) adds items to what is inside, never letting the contents exceed the capacity.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public int getContents() returns how much is inside, and public int getSpace() returns how much room is left.

task: Write class Locker with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
A new Locker is empty. Storing more than fits fills it to capacity and discards the rest rather than overflowing.
The contents belong to the object, not to the store method. A count declared inside store is forgotten the moment store returns.
hints: The driver calls store TWICE and asks for the contents in between. A store method that keeps its running total in a local variable prints the first amount and then the second amount, never their sum.
Declaring int contents = 0; inside store creates a NEW variable that hides the field. It compiles, it runs, and the field stays at 0 forever.
getSpace is derived from the capacity and the contents. Storing it as a fourth field means two numbers that can disagree.

3.4.title: Constructors
3.4.name: Two Ways to Build
3.4.brief: A constructor has no return type. Give it one and it silently becomes an ordinary method with the same name as the class, the compiler accepts it, every object is built by the default constructor instead, and every field is 0 or null. There is no error message anywhere in that sentence, which is why it is worth a question of its own.
3.4.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Ticket. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Ticket(String event, int price) that stores both.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: A constructor Ticket(String event) that stores the event with a price of 10.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public String getEvent() and public int getPrice() return what was stored.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public String describe() returns the event, a space, then the price.

task: Write class Ticket with the two constructors and the methods described. No main method.
The one argument constructor should call the two argument one rather than repeating the assignments. this(event, 10); is how, and it must be the first statement.
A constructor is named exactly like the class and has NO return type, not even void.
hints: public void Ticket(String event, int price) is NOT a constructor. It is a method that happens to share the name of the class, and every object then gets built by the invisible default constructor with all fields at 0 and null.
this(event, 10); calls your other constructor. It has to be the very first statement in the body.
The driver builds both kinds of Ticket. A one argument constructor that forgets the default price prints 0 rather than 10.

3.5.title: Methods: How to Write Them
3.5.name: Return, Do Not Print
3.5.brief: A void method that prints and an int method that returns look equally correct on a screen. Only one of them can be used by the code that called it. This question is graded entirely on what your methods hand back, so a class that prints the right answers scores zero, which is exactly what happens in May.
3.5.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Account. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Account(int balance) that stores the opening balance.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public void deposit(int amount) adds amount to the balance, ignoring any amount that is zero or negative.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public boolean withdraw(int amount) takes amount out and returns true, or changes nothing and returns false when the amount is more than the balance or is not positive.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public int getBalance() returns the current balance.

task: Write class Account with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
Part (c) returns whether the withdrawal happened. A method that prints "declined" and returns nothing cannot be used by the driver at all.
A refused withdrawal must leave the balance untouched. Deducting and then refusing is the bug this part is looking for.
hints: The driver withdraws the SAME amount twice. If the first succeeds and drains the account, the second must return false and leave the balance where it is.
Deducting first and checking afterwards leaves the balance wrong on every refusal, and the getBalance line right after the false is where it shows.
A withdrawal of exactly the whole balance is allowed. Only more than the balance is refused.

3.6.title: Methods: Passing and Returning Object References
3.6.name: The Half Fix
3.6.brief: When a method returns the object's own array, the caller can change the object from outside it, and nothing in the class can stop them. Students usually find half of this: they copy on the way OUT and not on the way IN, or the reverse. A half fixed class is what actually gets handed in, so that is what this question is built to detect.
3.6.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Roster. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Roster(int[] scores) that stores a COPY of the array it is given.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public int[] getScores() returns a COPY of the stored array.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public int get(int index) returns the stored value at that index.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public int size() returns how many scores are stored.

task: Write class Roster with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
Both directions need a copy. The driver changes the array it handed you AND changes the array you handed back, then asks what you have stored.
Copy by looping and assigning element by element. A new array of the same length, filled in a loop, is all that is needed.
hints: The driver pokes at the array it gave you, then pokes at the array you gave it, and asks for element 0 after each. Only a class that copied in BOTH directions gives the same answer all three times.
this.scores = scores; stores the caller's array itself, not a copy. Every later change they make is a change to your object.
A copy is a new array plus a loop. new int[scores.length] then assign each element across.

3.7.title: Class Variables and Methods
3.7.name: Shared or Not
3.7.brief: A static field belongs to the class and an instance field belongs to each object, and choosing wrong produces a counter that says 1 forever or a serial number that every object shares. Both compile. Both look right until you build the second object, which is why the driver here builds three.
3.7.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Badge. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Badge(String name) that stores the name and assigns this badge the next serial number, starting at 1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public String getName() and public int getSerial() return this badge's own values.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int getIssued() returns how many Badge objects have been made in total.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static void reset() sets the issued count back to 0, so the next badge is serial 1 again.

task: Write class Badge with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
The count of badges issued belongs to the CLASS. The serial number belongs to each OBJECT.
Part (c) and part (d) are static, so they are called on Badge itself rather than on a badge.
hints: The driver prints the serial of the FIRST badge after building the second. If the serial is static, both badges share it and the first one has silently changed.
The count is incremented before the serial is read, which is what makes the first badge serial 1 rather than 0.
A static method cannot read an instance field, and the compiler will say so. That error is a useful signal that you put a field on the wrong side.

3.8.title: Scope and Access
3.8.name: What the Name Reaches
3.8.brief: Which variable a name reaches is decided by where it was declared, not by what it is called. A parameter named like a field hides that field for the whole method, and the method still compiles and still runs. Every part of this question is a place that mistake can hide.
3.8.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Counter. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Counter(int start, int step) that stores both, where step is how much each bump adds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public void bump() adds step to the current value.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public void bumpBy(int step) adds THAT step to the current value, without changing the stored step.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public int getValue() and public int getStep() return the current value and the stored step.

task: Write class Counter with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
Part (c) takes a parameter called step, which hides the field of the same name for that whole method. Adding the parameter is correct here; changing the FIELD is not.
After a call to bumpBy, getStep must still return the value the constructor was given.
hints: The driver calls bump AFTER bumpBy and asks for the value again. If bumpBy overwrote the stored step, that last bump adds the wrong amount and the mistake finally becomes visible.
Inside bumpBy, the bare name step means the parameter. To reach the field you would have to write this.step, which is exactly what this method must NOT change.
The constructor has the same collision. this.step = step; assigns the parameter to the field; step = step; assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field at 0.

3.9.title: The this Keyword
3.9.name: Which Object Am I
3.9.brief: this is the object the method was called on, and it becomes necessary the moment a method takes another object of the same class as a parameter. Inside a comparison of two Points, a bare field name means MINE and the parameter's field means theirs, and getting that backwards produces an answer that is right whenever the two happen to be equal.
3.9.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Point. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A constructor Point(int x, int y) that stores both, using this to tell the parameters from the fields.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public int getX() and public int getY() return this point's coordinates.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public boolean sameAs(Point other) returns whether both coordinates match.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public int distanceTo(Point other) returns the horizontal distance plus the vertical distance, never negative.

task: Write class Point with the constructor and methods described. No main method.
In part (c) and part (d), the bare names x and y mean THIS point. The other point's values come through other.
Part (d) must never be negative. Math.abs on each difference does that without an if.
hints: The driver measures the distance in BOTH directions. A method that subtracts without taking the magnitude gives a negative answer one of those two times.
A constructor whose parameters are named like its fields needs this on the left of each assignment. Without it, both assignments do nothing at all.
Comparing two points needs both coordinates. Checking only x is correct whenever the y values happen to agree, which is exactly the kind of nearly right the hidden cases are built to catch.

4.1.title: Ethical and Social Issues Around Data Collection
4.1.name: Aggregate, Do Not Identify
4.1.brief: The ethical rule in this topic has a concrete programming shape: report the aggregate, not the individual. A count that can only be satisfied by one person is not anonymous, and this question asks you to detect exactly that, which is what a real suppression rule does.
4.1.given: The driver builds an int array of counts, one per group, and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Report. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int total(int[] counts) returns the sum of every count.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int groups(int[] counts) returns how many groups there are.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static boolean isIdentifying(int[] counts, int minimum) returns whether ANY group has a count below minimum but above 0.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int suppressed(int[] counts, int minimum) returns the total of only the groups that are at or above minimum.

task: Write class Report with the four static methods described. No main method.
A group with a count of 0 is not identifying, because nobody is in it. Only a small NON EMPTY group is.
Part (d) leaves out the small groups entirely rather than replacing them with zero after the fact.
hints: An enhanced for loop reads every element and is the right tool whenever you do not need the index. Part (a), (c) and (d) never need one.
Part (c) has two conditions joined by and: above zero AND below the minimum. Dropping the first makes every empty group look identifying.
Part (d) is a filtered sum. The groups below the minimum contribute nothing rather than contributing zero after being counted.

4.2.title: Introduction to Using Data Sets
4.2.name: Summarising a Data Set
4.2.brief: The first thing anyone does with a data set is ask for its minimum, maximum and mean, and the first bug anyone writes is seeding the maximum at 0. On data that is entirely negative that reports a maximum which is not in the data at all, and no error is raised.
4.2.given: The driver builds an int array and passes it to your methods. Every array has at least one element. Write a class named Summary. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int max(int[] data) returns the largest value.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int min(int[] data) returns the smallest value.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int range(int[] data) returns the largest minus the smallest.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int mean(int[] data) returns the sum divided by the length, using integer division.

task: Write class Summary with the four static methods described. No main method.
Seed the maximum and the minimum with the FIRST element, never with 0. The array may be entirely negative or entirely positive.
Parts (a) and (b) should be written once each and reused by part (c).
hints: Seeding with data[0] and starting the loop at 1 is the standard shape. It works for any data because the seed is guaranteed to be a real element.
A maximum seeded at 0 is correct only when the data happens to contain something positive. The hidden cases here do not.
Part (c) is one line if parts (a) and (b) are right. Re-scanning the array a third time is another chance to seed one of them wrongly.

4.3.title: Array Creation and Access
4.3.name: Index Boundaries
4.3.brief: Valid indexes run from 0 to length - 1. Everything in this topic follows from that one sentence, and every bug in it is a place where length was used as if it were an index.
4.3.given: The driver builds an int array and passes it to your methods. Every array has at least one element. Write a class named Access. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int first(int[] data) returns the first element.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int last(int[] data) returns the last element.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static boolean isValid(int[] data, int index) returns whether index is a usable index for data.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int at(int[] data, int index) returns the element at index, or -1 when the index is not usable.

task: Write class Access with the four static methods described. No main method.
A negative index is not usable either. Part (c) has to rule out both ends.
Part (d) must not throw. Check with part (c) before reaching into the array.
hints: data[data.length] is always out of bounds. The last element is at data.length - 1.
Part (c) needs both halves. index < data.length alone accepts -1, which throws the moment part (d) uses it.
The driver probes with an index that is sometimes valid and sometimes not, so both answers from part (d) are checked.

4.4.title: Traversing Arrays
4.4.name: Forwards and Backwards
4.4.brief: A backwards traversal starts at length - 1 and a forwards one stops before length, and writing either bound the other way round is the crash this topic is famous for. An enhanced for loop avoids both, at the cost of not knowing where it is.
4.4.given: The driver builds an int array and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Traverse. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static String forwards(int[] data) returns every element separated by single spaces, or the empty String for an empty array.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static String backwards(int[] data) returns every element in reverse, separated by single spaces.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int sumEvenIndexes(int[] data) returns the sum of the elements at indexes 0, 2, 4 and so on.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int countMatching(int[] data, int target) returns how many elements equal target.

task: Write class Traverse with the four static methods described. No main method.
Parts (a) and (b) put a single space BETWEEN elements and none at the start.
Part (c) is about the INDEX being even, not the value.
hints: A backwards loop starts at data.length - 1 and continues while the index is at least 0. Starting at data.length throws on the very first pass.
Part (c) steps the index by 2. The elements at odd indexes are skipped entirely, whatever their values.
The separator goes before every element except the one that comes first in the output, which is a different element in part (a) and part (b).

4.5.title: Algorithms with Arrays
4.5.name: Which One Won
4.5.brief: This is where the tie breaking rule finally becomes gradeable. Returning the VALUE of the largest element hides whether you kept the first or the last one; returning its INDEX does not. A strict greater-than keeps the earlier index and a greater-or-equal keeps the later one, and the exam always says which it wants.
4.5.given: The driver builds an int array and passes it to your methods. Every array has at least one element. Write a class named Find. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int indexOfMax(int[] data) returns the index of the largest value, and the SMALLEST such index when it appears more than once.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int indexOfLastMax(int[] data) returns the LARGEST index at which the largest value appears.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int indexOf(int[] data, int target) returns the first index holding target, or -1 when it is absent.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static boolean isSorted(int[] data) returns whether the values never decrease from left to right.

task: Write class Find with the four static methods described. No main method.
Parts (a) and (b) differ ONLY in their tie breaking. One uses a strict comparison and the other does not.
A one element array is sorted, and so is an array whose values are all equal.
hints: Track the INDEX of the best element rather than its value. Comparing data[i] to data[best] keeps both facts in one variable.
A strict > never replaces on a tie, so the earliest winner survives. A >= replaces every time, so the latest one does.
Part (d) compares each element to the one before it. Values that are equal do not break the ordering, so the test is < and not <=.

4.6.title: Using Text Files
4.6.name: Parsing Lines
4.6.brief: Reading a file and reading standard input are the same problem once the data is in hand: text arrives as Strings and has to become numbers before it can be added up. "12" + "3" is "123", and that is the bug this topic exists to prevent.
4.6.given: The driver reads whitespace separated tokens and passes them to your methods as a String array. Write a class named Lines. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int count(String[] tokens) returns how many tokens there are.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int sum(String[] tokens) returns the sum of the tokens read as integers.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static String join(String[] tokens) returns the tokens separated by commas, with no comma at the start or end.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int longest(String[] tokens) returns the length of the longest token, and 0 when there are none.

task: Write class Lines with the four static methods described. No main method.
Every token is a valid integer, so Integer.parseInt will not throw.
Part (b) must ADD the numbers. Concatenating the Strings and parsing at the end is a different, much larger number.
hints: Integer.parseInt turns one token into a number. Parse each token as you go and add the numbers, rather than gluing the text together first.
Part (d) can seed at 0 safely, because a length is never negative. That is the one place in this unit where a zero seed is correct.
The comma in part (c) goes between tokens. Adding it after every token leaves one on the end, which the driver compares.

4.7.title: Wrapper Classes
4.7.name: Integer Is Not int
4.7.brief: Two Integer objects holding the same number can be different objects, and == compares objects rather than values. Java caches the small ones, so == is true up to 127 and false at 128, which is the most reliably surprising fact in the whole course. equals is always right.
4.7.given: The driver passes you ints and Integer objects. Write a class named Boxes. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static boolean sameValue(Integer a, Integer b) returns whether the two hold the same number, correctly for every value.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int unbox(Integer a) returns the int inside.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static Integer box(int a) returns an Integer holding that value.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int sum(Integer a, Integer b) returns the sum of the two values.

task: Write class Boxes with the four static methods described. No main method.
Part (a) must be right for large values too. The driver deliberately tests numbers on both sides of the cache boundary.
Autoboxing does parts (b), (c) and (d) for you. The point of the question is part (a).
hints: a.equals(b) compares the values inside. a == b compares whether they are the same object, which is true for small cached values and false for large ones.
The driver builds one Integer with new, which ALWAYS makes a fresh object. Comparing it with == is false even when the number matches.
Parts (b), (c) and (d) need no conversion code. Java boxes and unboxes automatically wherever the types line up.

4.8.title: ArrayList Methods
4.8.name: Add, Set, Remove
4.8.brief: An ArrayList shifts. add at an index pushes everything right, remove at an index pulls everything left, and set replaces without moving anything. Confusing set with add at the same index changes the size, which is the difference the exam looks for.
4.8.given: The driver builds an ArrayList of Integer and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Editor. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int size(ArrayList<Integer> list) returns how many elements it holds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static void appendTwice(ArrayList<Integer> list, int value) adds value to the END of the list twice.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static void replaceFirst(ArrayList<Integer> list, int value) replaces the element at index 0 without changing the size. Do nothing when the list is empty.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int removeLast(ArrayList<Integer> list) removes and returns the last element, or returns -1 and changes nothing when the list is empty.

task: Write class Editor with the four static methods described. No main method.
These methods change the list they are GIVEN. An ArrayList is an object, so the caller sees the change.
Part (c) uses set and not add. add at index 0 pushes the old element aside and makes the list longer.
hints: set(0, value) replaces. add(0, value) inserts. The driver prints the whole list right after, so a size that grew by one is immediately visible.
remove(index) returns the element it removed, so part (d) needs no separate get.
The last index is size() - 1. Using size() throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

4.9.title: Traversing ArrayLists
4.9.name: Removing While Looping
4.9.brief: Removing from a list while walking it forward skips the element that slides into the gap. It is not a crash and not an exception; it is a quietly wrong answer that only shows when two removable elements sit next to each other. Every hidden case here has exactly that.
4.9.given: The driver builds an ArrayList of Integer and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Prune. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int sum(ArrayList<Integer> list) returns the total of every element.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int countAbove(ArrayList<Integer> list, int threshold) returns how many elements are strictly greater than threshold.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static void removeAllEqual(ArrayList<Integer> list, int target) removes EVERY element equal to target.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int firstIndexAbove(ArrayList<Integer> list, int threshold) returns the first index holding a value above threshold, or -1.

task: Write class Prune with the four static methods described. No main method.
Part (c) must remove every match, including two that are adjacent. Walking backwards, or not advancing after a removal, both work.
Part (d) stops at the first match.
hints: Walking backwards is the simplest fix: removing an element only shifts the ones AFTER it, and you have already passed those.
Going forwards, the fix is to not increment the index after a removal, because a new element has just slid into that position.
Two adjacent matches are what expose the bug. One match on its own is removed correctly by both the right and the wrong loop.

4.10.title: Algorithms with ArrayLists
4.10.name: Build a New List
4.10.brief: Filtering into a NEW list is safer than editing in place and is what most free response questions ask for. The trap is returning the list you were given, or building the new one but never returning it, both of which look finished on the page.
4.10.given: The driver builds an ArrayList of Integer and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Build. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static ArrayList<Integer> above(ArrayList<Integer> list, int threshold) returns a NEW list of the elements strictly greater than threshold, in their original order.

parts.label: (b)
