parts.text: public static ArrayList<Integer> doubled(ArrayList<Integer> list) returns a NEW list with every element multiplied by 2, leaving the original alone.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static ArrayList<Integer> reversed(ArrayList<Integer> list) returns a NEW list in the opposite order.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int countDistinctValues(ArrayList<Integer> list) returns how many different values appear.

task: Write class Build with the four static methods described. No main method.
The original list must be unchanged after every one of these calls. The driver prints it again at the end to check.
Part (d) counts VALUES, so a list of 4, 4, 7 has two distinct values.
hints: Start each method with a brand new ArrayList and add into that. Returning the parameter hands back the caller's own list.
The driver prints the ORIGINAL list last. If any of your methods edited it in place, that final line is wrong even when the earlier ones looked right.
contains asks whether a value is already in a list, which is all part (d) needs.

4.11.title: 2D Array Creation and Access
4.11.name: Row Then Column
4.11.brief: grid[r][c] is row first and column second, and every grid in this question is deliberately NOT square. On a 3 by 3 grid a swapped pair of indexes quietly transposes the answer and every test still passes; on a 2 by 4 grid it throws immediately. That is the entire reason these dimensions are what they are.
4.11.given: The driver builds a rectangular 2D int array and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Cells. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int rows(int[][] grid) returns how many rows there are.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int cols(int[][] grid) returns how many columns each row has. Assume at least one row.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int at(int[][] grid, int r, int c) returns the value at row r and column c.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int corners(int[][] grid) returns the sum of the four corner values.

task: Write class Cells with the four static methods described. No main method.
grid.length is the number of ROWS. grid[0].length is the number of COLUMNS.
A grid with one row or one column still has four corners; some of them are the same cell.
hints: grid.length counts the rows because a 2D array is an array OF rows. Each row is itself an array, so grid[0].length counts the columns.
Swapping r and c in part (c) throws on a non square grid rather than returning the wrong number, which is a kinder failure than it looks.
On a grid with a single row, the top and bottom corners are the same two cells, so two values get counted twice. That is what the question asks for.

4.12.title: Traversing 2D Arrays
4.12.name: Row Major and Column Major
4.12.brief: Row major walks each row left to right; column major walks each column top to bottom. They visit the same cells in a different ORDER, and on a non square grid swapping the loop bounds is not merely a different order but an immediate crash.
4.12.given: The driver builds a rectangular 2D int array and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Walk. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static String rowMajor(int[][] grid) returns every value in row major order, separated by single spaces.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static String columnMajor(int[][] grid) returns every value in column major order, separated by single spaces.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int rowSum(int[][] grid, int r) returns the sum of row r.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int colSum(int[][] grid, int c) returns the sum of column c.

task: Write class Walk with the four static methods described. No main method.
Part (b) needs the column loop on the OUTSIDE and must still bound each index by its own dimension.
Separate the values with single spaces and do not start with one.
hints: The outer loop decides the order. Row major has rows outside; column major has columns outside. The index bounds do not swap with them.
A row sum walks the columns and a column sum walks the rows. That is easy to write backwards, and on a non square grid it throws rather than answering wrongly.
Both traversals visit every cell exactly once, so the two Strings contain the same numbers in a different order. If yours do not, one of them has a bound wrong.

4.13.title: Implementing 2D Array Algorithms
4.13.name: Finding in a Grid
4.13.brief: Searching a grid means returning WHERE something is, and a position is two numbers. This question asks for the row and the column separately so that a transposed answer is visibly wrong rather than accidentally right.
4.13.given: The driver builds a rectangular 2D int array and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Search2D. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int maxValue(int[][] grid) returns the largest value anywhere in the grid.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int rowOfMax(int[][] grid) returns the row index of the largest value, choosing the earliest in row major order on a tie.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int colOfMax(int[][] grid) returns the column index of that same cell.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int countEqual(int[][] grid, int target) returns how many cells hold target.

task: Write class Search2D with the four static methods described. No main method.
Seed the search with the cell at row 0 column 0, never with 0.
Parts (b) and (c) must describe the SAME cell. Searching twice invites them to disagree on a tie.
hints: Track the best POSITION rather than the best value, then read the value back out of the grid. That keeps parts (a), (b) and (c) describing one cell.
A strict greater-than keeps the first cell found in row major order, which is what the tie breaking rule asks for.
Seeding at grid[0][0] rather than 0 matters here for the same reason it did in 4.2: the grid may be entirely negative.

4.14.title: Searching Algorithms
4.14.name: Linear and Binary
4.14.brief: Binary search halves the range each pass, and every bug in it is a bound that fails to shrink. This question asks for the number of comparisons alongside the answer, so a search that finds the right element by doing linear work is visibly not a binary search.
4.14.given: The driver builds a SORTED int array and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Searcher. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int linear(int[] data, int target) returns the first index holding target, or -1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int binary(int[] data, int target) returns AN index holding target, or -1. The array is sorted.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int binarySteps(int[] data, int target) returns how many times the loop body of your binary search runs.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static boolean contains(int[] data, int target) returns whether target is present.

task: Write class Searcher with the four static methods described. No main method.
A binary search keeps a low and a high index and moves one of them PAST the midpoint every pass. Setting low = mid rather than mid + 1 never terminates.
Part (c) counts the passes of the same loop, so it must have the same shape as part (b).
hints: The driver prints whether the binary search FOUND the target rather than which index it landed on, because with repeated values a correct binary search may legitimately return any of them.
The step count is what separates a real binary search from a loop wearing its name. On sixteen sorted elements a binary search never needs more than five passes.
Move low to mid + 1 and high to mid - 1. Using mid itself leaves the range the same size and the loop never ends.

4.15.title: Sorting Algorithms
4.15.name: Selection and Insertion
4.15.brief: A swap needs a temporary. Writing a = b; b = a; loses one of the values before the second line runs, and the array ends up with a duplicate rather than a swap. That is the same bug as the one in 2.1, now inside a sort where it is much harder to see.
4.15.given: The driver builds an int array and passes it to your methods. Write a class named Sorter. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static void swap(int[] data, int i, int j) exchanges the two elements.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int indexOfMinFrom(int[] data, int start) returns the index of the smallest element at or after start.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static void selectionSort(int[] data) sorts the array ascending, using parts (a) and (b).

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static String show(int[] data) returns the elements separated by single spaces.

task: Write class Sorter with the four static methods described. No main method.
Part (a) needs a temporary variable. Without one the two elements both end up holding the same value.
The array is sorted IN PLACE, so the caller sees the change.
hints: The driver swaps the same pair TWICE, which should put the array back exactly as it was. A swap without a temporary fails that immediately.
Selection sort only needs to run to the second to last element, because once everything before it is placed the last one has nowhere else to go.
indexOfMinFrom seeds at start rather than at 0, which is what makes each pass ignore the part already sorted.

4.16.title: Recursion
4.16.name: Base Cases That Return the Right Thing
4.16.brief: A missing base case makes recursion crash, and everyone learns to look for that. A base case that returns the WRONG VALUE is the mistake that actually appears on student work: the method terminates, the recursion is shaped correctly, and every answer is off by the same factor. A sum that bottoms out at 1 and a product that bottoms out at 0 are the same error.
4.16.given: Nothing is given. Write a class named Recurse. Assume n is at least 0. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int sumTo(int n) returns 1 + 2 + ... + n recursively, and 0 when n is 0.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: public static int factorial(int n) returns n! recursively, and 1 when n is 0.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: public static int countDigits(int n) returns how many digits n has, recursively. The number 0 has one digit.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: public static int power(int base, int exp) returns base to the exp, recursively, and 1 when exp is 0.

task: Write class Recurse with the four static methods described. No main method.
Every part here has a base case that must return a SPECIFIC value. A sum bottoms out at 0 and a product bottoms out at 1, and swapping those two is the whole question.
Every recursive call must move toward the base case, or the method never returns.
hints: The base case value is the identity of whatever the recursion combines. Addition combines with 0 and multiplication combines with 1.
Part (c) bottoms out at any single digit number, which includes 0. Testing n == 0 instead throws away the last digit of every number.
The recursive call must be smaller. n - 1 and n / 10 both reach their base cases; n itself never does.

4.17.title: Recursive Searching and Sorting
4.17.name: Recursion That Returns
4.17.brief: The last topic of the course closes the thread opened in 1.10: a call whose result is discarded does nothing. In recursion that mistake is deadly, because the answer is built entirely out of returned values. Writing helper(...) on a line by itself instead of return helper(...) compiles, terminates, and answers wrongly every time.
4.17.given: The driver builds a SORTED int array and passes it to your methods. Write a class named RecSearch. Do not write a main method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: public static int find(int[] data, int target, int low, int high) searches recursively between low and high inclusive and returns an index holding target, or -1.

parts.label: (b)

parts.text: public static int maxFrom(int[] data, int i) returns the largest value at or after index i, recursively. Assume i is a valid index.

parts.text: public static int countFrom(int[] data, int target, int i) returns how many elements at or after i equal target, recursively.

task: Write class RecSearch with the four methods described. No main method.
Every recursive call's result must be RETURNED or combined into the answer. Calling and discarding compiles and answers wrongly.
Part (a) returns -1 when low passes high, which is what makes the search end when the target is absent.
hints: Two methods with the same name and different parameter lists are overloads, and the short one exists only to supply the starting bounds to the long one.
Part (c) and part (d) both compute the answer for the REST of the array first, then fold the current element into it. That returned value is the whole answer.
The driver prints whether the search succeeded rather than the index, because on repeated values a correct recursive search may land on any of them.
